name: Moclobemide (Manerix)
summary: Reversible MAO-A inhibitor (RIMA) antidepressant used for unipolar major depression. Often easier on food restrictions than older MAOIs, but drug interactions are still a big deal.
description: Moclobemide is an antidepressant used for moderate to severe unipolar depression in adults (not available in the U.S.). It’s a reversible MAOI, which means it boosts serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine by temporarily blocking the MAO-A enzyme that breaks them down. Many people notice early changes in 1–2 weeks, with fuller benefits building over 4–6 weeks. You still have to take interactions seriously—mixing it with certain antidepressants, opioids like meperidine, dextromethorphan, tramadol, or triptans can be dangerous. It’s usually taken right after meals.
patient_summary: Moclobemide is a reversible MAOI antidepressant used for unipolar depression (not sold in the U.S.). It can start helping within 1–2 weeks, with bigger improvements over 4–6 weeks. You generally don’t need a strict tyramine diet like older MAOIs, but you DO need to respect the interaction list—mixing it with SSRIs/SNRIs, certain pain meds, dextromethorphan, tramadol, or triptans can be risky. Take it after meals and don’t stop suddenly after longer use—taper it down.

primary_indications: Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar) in adults (moderate to severe)

linked_conditions.context: Used for unipolar major depression in adults. Typically considered when a person has not done well with (or can’t tolerate) more common antidepressants, or when an MAOI-style mechanism is clinically desired.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to moclobemide or any component of the formulation
Concurrent use with conventional (irreversible) monoamine oxidase inhibitors

efficacy_response.patient_text: This isn’t a “take it today, feel different tonight” medication. Some people notice early shifts (less heaviness, better energy, slightly clearer thinking) in the first 1–2 weeks, but the real antidepressant effect typically builds over 4–6 weeks.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Approximately ~55% after a single dose; increases substantially with repeated dosing
pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: early effects may show up in 1–2 weeks; continued improvement through 4–6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Terminal elimination ~1.5 hours (can be longer in hepatic impairment)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic (oxidative metabolism); partial involvement of CYP2C19 and CYP2D6
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Administer after meals; taking after meals can reduce the chance of tyramine-related reactions and is the standard administration advice

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Moclobemide is used to treat unipolar major depression in adults (moderate to severe). It’s not a U.S. medication, but it’s used in other countries as a reversible MAOI option. In psychiatry terms: it’s for depression that’s dragging your mood, energy, sleep, motivation, and ability to function.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar)}: Moderate to severe depression in adults

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Real-life experience varies, but these are the patterns clinicians hear about most often:

quotes: Week 2 felt like the fog started thinning—still there, just not glued to my face.
I didn’t wake up “happy,” but I stopped waking up hopeless.
It wasn’t fireworks. It was quieter: I could do things again.
items.note: Early changes often show up in 1–2 weeks, with stronger improvement over 4–6 weeks.

quotes: The first week I felt a little wired—like my body got the memo before my mood did.
More restless than usual at the start, then it settled.
I had a few days of extra anxiety and irritability, then it smoothed out.
items.note: Agitation, restlessness, and insomnia can happen—particularly during startup or dose increases.

quotes: I slept lighter at first—more tossing and turning.
Dreams got vivid. Not always fun.
Once my mood improved, my sleep followed.
items.note: Insomnia and sleep disturbance are reported. If sleep gets worse, it’s a signal to reassess dose timing, pace of titration, and overall fit.

quotes: I liked that it’s an MAOI that’s not as food-restrictive, but the drug interaction list is no joke.
I had to triple-check cough meds and migraine meds.
My prescriber drilled one rule: don’t freestyle combinations.
items.note: Food tyramine restriction usually isn’t strict like older MAOIs, but medication interactions can be serious.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Moclobemide works on neurotransmitters quickly in the body, but mood improvement still takes time—like other antidepressants.
key_points: 0.5–3.5 hours: Peaks in the bloodstream after a dose
1–2 weeks: Early improvement may be noticeable for some people
4–6 weeks: Continued improvement often builds over time
~1.5 hours: Terminal elimination half-life (short), but the clinical effect lasts longer than the blood level suggests
Take after meals: This is standard for administration and may reduce tyramine-related reactions

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Moclobemide is a legitimate antidepressant option for unipolar depression, but it’s not a “quick fix.” The most realistic timeline is early shifts in 1–2 weeks (energy, motivation, less emotional weight), then steadier improvement through weeks 4–6. If nothing is moving by that point, the plan usually needs adjustment—dose, diagnosis check (including bipolar screening), psychotherapy support, or a different medication strategy.
sections.clinical_details: Response tends to be gradual. Early activation (restlessness, insomnia, anxiety) can occur during initiation or dose increases and doesn’t automatically mean the medication is failing—sometimes it settles as the nervous system adapts. That said, significant agitation, hypomania, or worsening suicidality is a stop-and-reassess moment.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Do not combine moclobemide with serotonergic antidepressants or certain pain/cough/migraine meds. The interaction risk is the main safety issue here.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (18 to 24 years of age) with major depressive disorder and other psychiatric disorders. Monitor closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior, especially during the first 1 to 2 months of therapy and during dose changes.
other: Serotonin syndrome risk: Can be life-threatening when combined with serotonergic agents (SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, triptans, lithium, buspirone, St. John’s wort, tryptophan, certain opioids).
Mania/hypomania risk: Can precipitate mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. Screen before prescribing and avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder.
CNS effects: May cause sedation or cognitive slowing in some people—use caution with driving or tasks requiring sharp focus until you know your response.
Ocular effects: Can cause mild pupillary dilation and may trigger angle-closure in susceptible individuals with narrow-angle glaucoma risk.
Hepatic impairment: Clearance decreases and blood levels can rise substantially in chronic liver disease; dose reduction is required in severe impairment.
Discontinuation syndrome: Abrupt stopping can cause significant neuropsychiatric withdrawal symptoms; taper gradually after longer treatment.
Hypertensive reactions: Less food-sensitive than older MAOIs for most people, but still educate on symptoms like occipital headache, neck stiffness, palpitations, and unusual blood pressure changes.
patient_counseling: Before taking anything new (cold meds, cough syrups, migraine meds, pain meds, supplements), ask your prescriber or pharmacist. This is not a medication to “just mix and hope.”
If you develop agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, muscle stiffness, severe diarrhea, or feel suddenly “wired and unwell,” get urgent help—those can be serotonin syndrome red flags.
If your mood flips into hypomania/mania (sleeping less but feeling energized, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior), stop and contact your clinician ASAP.
Take moclobemide right after meals as directed.
If you have liver disease, your dosing needs extra caution—don’t assume “standard dose” applies.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues are sleep disruption, restlessness/anxiety activation, GI symptoms, and tremor. A smaller number of people notice cardiovascular effects like palpitations or blood pressure changes.
plain_language_list: Agitation, restlessness, nervousness, or increased anxiety (especially early)
GI upset (constipation, diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, heartburn-type symptoms)

common.patient_note: If sleep gets worse after starting or increasing the dose, it can help to slow titration and avoid late-day dosing. Persistent insomnia is a reason to reassess the plan.
Some people feel activated early on—more jittery, keyed up, or irritable. Mild activation can fade, but intense agitation, panic, or impulsivity needs urgent clinical attention.
A fine hand tremor can happen, especially during dose changes. Let your prescriber know if it interferes with daily function.
Taking it immediately after meals can help with tolerability for some people.
If you get persistent racing heart, chest pain, fainting, or severe blood pressure symptoms, treat that as urgent.

serious: Serotonin syndrome (especially with interacting meds): agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, rigidity, diarrhea, seizures. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Suicidal ideation or sudden worsening depression, especially early in treatment or during dose changes: seek urgent support.
Mania/hypomania switch (especially if bipolar disorder is present): decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, racing thoughts, risky behavior—urgent reassessment needed.
Hypertensive reaction (uncommon, but possible): severe headache (often back of head), neck stiffness, palpitations, blood pressure spikes—urgent evaluation.
Liver enzyme elevations (reported postmarketing): monitor if symptoms of liver injury occur (jaundice, dark urine, severe fatigue, right upper abdominal pain).

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Moclobemide is a reversible MAO-A inhibitor. That still means serious interaction potential—especially with serotonergic meds and certain opioids/cough/migraine meds. This is the part you take personally.

items.risk: High risk of serotonin syndrome and other severe reactions.
items.action: Avoid combination. When switching between antidepressants, use appropriate washout periods (see below).
Avoid combination. Use washout periods when switching.

items.risk: Serotonin syndrome risk and increased triptan exposure.
items.action: Contraindicated—choose an alternative migraine strategy with your prescriber.

items.risk: Serotonin syndrome and opioid-related toxicity risk.
Severe, potentially life-threatening reactions with MAO inhibition.
Serious interaction risk; combination not recommended/contraindicated in many product labels.
items.action: Do not combine unless a specialist explicitly directs it (and typically, this combination is avoided).

items.with: Other MAOIs (including selegiline; and non-psychiatric MAOI-like agents such as linezolid or IV methylene blue)
items.risk: Excessive MAO inhibition and severe adverse reactions (including serotonin syndrome/hypertensive events).
items.action: Avoid combination. If linezolid/IV methylene blue is needed, moclobemide is typically stopped and urgent medical coordination is required.

items.with: St. John’s wort, tryptophan, and other serotonergic supplements
items.action: Avoid unless your clinician specifically approves.

items.risk: Moclobemide can inhibit CYP2C19 (moderate) and CYP2D6 (weak), which can raise levels of some other medications.
items.action: Medication list review matters—dose adjustments or alternatives may be needed.

items.risk: Unlike older irreversible MAOIs, strict tyramine restriction usually isn’t required, but unusual reactions are still possible.
items.action: Take moclobemide after meals and know warning symptoms (occipital headache, neck stiffness, palpitations, unusual BP symptoms). If symptoms occur, seek medical advice.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on moclobemide for a while, don’t stop it abruptly. MAOI-class antidepressants can cause a more intense discontinuation syndrome in some people, so a conservative taper is often the smarter move.
key_points: If treatment lasted 4+ weeks: taper gradually over about 2–4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to catch returning depression early.
If treatment lasted 2–3 weeks: taper over about 1–2 weeks is often reasonable.
If treatment lasted <2 weeks: a taper may not be necessary for many people (but individual sensitivity varies).
Go slower (4+ weeks) if you have a history of antidepressant withdrawal symptoms or you were on higher doses.
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: return to the previous dose and taper more gradually.
Some people on long-term treatment (>6 months), especially with past discontinuation syndrome, may benefit from a very slow taper over >3 months.

Possible discontinuation symptoms with MAOIs can include agitation, irritability, insomnia, confusion, mood worsening, hypomania/mania-like symptoms, and (rarely) more severe neurologic symptoms—so tapering isn’t just “comfort,” it’s safety.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Moclobemide dosing is typically started at 300 mg/day in divided doses, then adjusted based on response and tolerability. It should be taken immediately after meals.

adult.depression_initial: 300 mg/day PO in 2 divided doses (eg, 150 mg BID), taken immediately after meals
adult.depression_titration: May increase gradually beginning 1 week after starting therapy based on response and tolerability
adult.long_term_adjustment: Some people may be maintained on a lower daily dose long-term if symptoms remain controlled
adult.switching_washout_to_moclobemide: Allow 14 days after stopping most antidepressants without long half-life metabolites (eg, many TCAs, paroxetine, fluvoxamine, venlafaxine) or another MAOI before starting moclobemide; allow 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting moclobemide
adult.switching_washout_from_moclobemide: Allow at least 2 to 14 days after stopping moclobemide before starting another antidepressant or MAOI (based on the specific agent and clinical risk)

sections.simple_explanation: This medication is usually taken twice a day after meals. Dose increases are typically done gradually. Even though moclobemide has a short half-life, the antidepressant benefit builds over weeks, not hours.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Moclobemide requires extra caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding, liver disease, and in anyone with bipolar risk. It’s also not indicated for children and adolescents.
sections.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies have reported adverse events. In humans, risk-benefit decisions should be individualized, and alternatives with more established pregnancy safety data are often preferred when appropriate.
sections.lactation: Small quantities are excreted in breast milk. Breast-feeding is not recommended by the manufacturer.
sections.pediatrics: Not indicated. Safety and efficacy have not been established in patients under 18.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Start conservatively and monitor closely for activation, blood pressure effects, cognitive changes, and falls if sedation occurs.
sections.hepatic: Mild to moderate impairment: no specific adjustment provided in some labeling, but use caution because clearance can be reduced. Severe impairment: decrease daily dose to about 33% to 50% of the usual dose.
sections.renal: No manufacturer-provided adjustment in many labels; need for adjustment is considered unlikely based on available pharmacokinetic evidence. Use caution and monitor tolerability.
sections.slow_metabolizers: Slow CYP2C19 and/or CYP2D6 metabolizers may have higher serum concentrations (roughly ~1.5x AUC reported in some data). Consider slower titration and closer side-effect monitoring.
sections.bipolar_disorder: Not approved for bipolar depression. Screen for bipolar disorder before treatment; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder due to risk of mania/hypomania and mood destabilization.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidal ideation and behavioral changes: especially early (first 1–2 months) and during dose changes; involve family/caregivers when appropriate.
Mood polarity: monitor for hypomania/mania symptoms (reduced need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, impulsivity, grandiosity).
Serotonin syndrome surveillance: if any interacting medications/supplements are added or suspected; watch for agitation, confusion, autonomic instability, tremor/rigidity, GI symptoms, and seizures.
Blood pressure and cardiovascular symptoms: palpitations, tachycardia, blood pressure changes; educate on when symptoms are urgent.
Liver function tests: periodic monitoring, especially in those with liver disease or symptoms suggestive of hepatotoxicity.
Sleep and activation symptoms: insomnia, agitation, restlessness, anxiety spikes; consider dose timing, slower titration, or reassessment if severe.
Medication reconciliation at every visit: new prescriptions, OTC cold/cough meds, migraine meds, pain meds, supplements (this is a high-interaction medication).
Clinical response tracking: energy, motivation, anhedonia, concentration, and functioning over weeks 2–6 to confirm trajectory and adjust plan.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Moclobemide is available as oral tablets in several strengths depending on country and manufacturer. In Canada, Manerix is a common brand name.
items: Brand example (Canada): Manerix tablets (commonly 150 mg and 300 mg)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Moclobemide is a short-acting, reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type A (MAO-A). MAO-A normally breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. By temporarily blocking MAO-A, moclobemide increases the availability of these neurotransmitters, which can improve depressive symptoms over time.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Moclobemide sits in the “specialist toolbox” category. It’s an MAOI-style antidepressant (reversible MAO-A inhibitor), which can be appealing when someone hasn’t responded to more standard antidepressants or has a symptom pattern where MAOI mechanisms are being considered. Compared with older irreversible MAOIs, moclobemide is often viewed as less strict on tyramine food rules for many patients—but it still demands serious respect for drug interactions, washout periods, and careful switching. If there’s any bipolar risk, screening and a mood-stabilizer-informed plan matters.

seo.title: Moclobemide (Manerix): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, Interactions & Tapering
seo.description: Moclobemide (Manerix) is a reversible MAO-A inhibitor antidepressant used for unipolar depression (not available in the U.S.). Learn dosing (300–600 mg/day), onset (1–6 weeks), side effects, dangerous interactions, switching washouts, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Moclobemide is used to treat unipolar major depression in adults, especially moderate to severe cases. It’s a reversible MAO-A inhibitor (RIMA), meaning it increases serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine by temporarily blocking the enzyme that breaks them down.

faqs.q: How long does moclobemide take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes within 1–2 weeks, but fuller antidepressant benefit typically builds over 4–6 weeks. If nothing is improving by that point, it’s time to reassess the plan with your prescriber.

faqs.q: Is moclobemide available in the United States?
faqs.a: No. Moclobemide is not available in the U.S. It is available in other countries (including Canada under brand names like Manerix and ALTI-Moclobemide).

faqs.q: Do I need a strict tyramine diet like older MAOIs?
faqs.a: Usually, moclobemide doesn’t require the same strict tyramine food restrictions as older irreversible MAOIs. But you still need to know the warning symptoms of a reaction—occipital headache, neck stiffness, palpitations, unusual blood pressure symptoms—and you should take it immediately after meals as directed.

faqs.q: What medications absolutely should not be mixed with moclobemide?
faqs.a: Key ones include SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic/tetracyclic antidepressants, other MAOIs, tramadol, meperidine, dextromethorphan (many cough syrups), triptans (migraine meds), and several others listed as contraindicated in product labeling. The big risks are serotonin syndrome and other severe reactions.

faqs.q: How do switching washout periods work with moclobemide?
faqs.a: When switching to moclobemide from many antidepressants or another MAOI, a 14-day washout is commonly used (and 5 weeks after fluoxetine because it lingers). When switching from moclobemide to another antidepressant/MAOI, many references recommend at least 2–14 days depending on the next medication and clinical risk. Your prescriber should give you a specific plan—this is not a DIY zone.

faqs.q: Can moclobemide make anxiety or insomnia worse at first?
faqs.a: Yes. Activation symptoms like agitation, increased anxiety, restlessness, and insomnia can happen early on or after dose increases. Mild activation may settle, but severe agitation, panic symptoms, or impulsive behavior is a red-flag reason to contact your clinician quickly.

Moclobemide alone usually doesn’t cause serotonin syndrome, but the risk rises sharply if it’s combined with serotonergic agents (like SSRIs/SNRIs, tramadol, triptans, lithium, buspirone, St. John’s wort, tryptophan, and certain opioids). Symptoms like confusion, agitation, fever, sweating, tremor, muscle stiffness, and severe diarrhea need urgent medical attention.

faqs.q: How do I taper off moclobemide safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4+ weeks, a gradual taper over about 2–4 weeks is commonly recommended to reduce withdrawal symptoms and detect returning depression. If you’ve had withdrawal issues before or were on higher doses, a slower taper may be needed. If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable, it’s often safer to return to the previous dose and taper more slowly.

faqs.q: Is moclobemide safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Animal studies have shown adverse events, and breastfeeding is not recommended by the manufacturer because small amounts can pass into breast milk. In real life, this becomes a personalized risk-benefit decision with your clinician, often favoring alternatives with more established safety data when appropriate.

It can. Like other antidepressants, moclobemide may trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. That’s why bipolar screening matters before starting, and why antidepressant monotherapy is generally avoided in bipolar disorder.
